content.title: Why Earth has seasons
content.explanation: Earth's axis is tilted 23.44°. As Earth orbits the Sun, each hemisphere leans toward the Sun for part of the year (summer: higher sun, longer days) and away for another part (winter: low sun, short days). Distance from the Sun barely matters - Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January, during the northern winter.
tryThis: Scrub through the orbit and watch the daylight hours for your latitude. When are they longest?
Set the tilt to 0°. What happens to the seasons and the daylight hours?
Compare noon sun altitude in June and December at your latitude, and check the beam spread: the same sunlight covers more ground when the Sun is low.
Watch the Earth-Sun distance across the year. Is Earth closest to the Sun in the northern summer or winter? Does distance explain seasons?
content.keyIdea: Seasons are caused by Earth's tilted axis changing the sun angle and day length, not by Earth's distance from the Sun.
